subChunks.title: Fetching Data from APIs
subChunks.hookHtml: Most real React apps consume data from a server. Fetching, tracking loading state, handling errors, and displaying the result are the four-step pattern every component that talks to an API must implement. Get this pattern right once and you'll use it everywhere.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The three-state pattern

Every data fetch has three possible states your UI must handle:

  • Loading — the request is in flight
  • Error — the request failed
  • Success — data is available
import { useState, useEffect } from 'react';

function UserProfile({ userId }) {
  const [user, setUser] = useState(null);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [error, setError] = useState(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    setLoading(true);
    setError(null);

    fetch(`https://api.example.com/users/${userId}`)
      .then(res => {
        if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
        return res.json();
      })
      .then(data => {
        setUser(data);
        setLoading(false);
      })
      .catch(err => {
        setError(err.message);
        setLoading(false);
      });
  }, [userId]);

  if (loading) return <p data-testid="loading">Loading...</p>;
  if (error)   return <p data-testid="error">Error: {error}</p>;
  return <div data-testid="user"><h2>{user.name}</h2></div>;
}

Using async/await with useEffect

You cannot make the effect callback itself async — it would return a Promise. Define an async function inside the effect and call it immediately:

useEffect(() => {
  async function loadUser() {
    try {
      setLoading(true);
      const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`);
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      const data = await res.json();
      setUser(data);
    } catch (err) {
      setError(err.message);
    } finally {
      setLoading(false);
    }
  }

  loadUser();
}, [userId]);

Avoiding race conditions with a cleanup flag

useEffect(() => {
  let cancelled = false;

  async function loadUser() {
    try {
      setLoading(true);
      const res = await fetch(`/api/users/${userId}`);
      const data = await res.json();
      if (!cancelled) setUser(data);
    } catch (err) {
      if (!cancelled) setError(err.message);
    } finally {
      if (!cancelled) setLoading(false);
    }
  }

  loadUser();
  return () => { cancelled = true; };
}, [userId]);

Vex: "Always reset loading and error state at the start of a new fetch. If you skip resetting error, a user who retried after an error will see the old error flash briefly before the new data arrives."

Using a public test API

jsonplaceholder.typicode.com provides free REST endpoints with realistic fake data:

// GET /posts — array of 100 posts
// GET /posts/1 — single post
// GET /users — array of 10 users
fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1')
  .then(r => r.json())
  .then(data => console.log(data));

storyBeats.text: A messenger raven arrives with a scroll. Vex holds it up: 'The Guild's quest board is now live — data from a real server. How do we display it?'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Every data fetch has three possible states: loading, error, and success. Your UI must handle all three. Show a spinner while loading. Show an error message if the request fails. Show the data when it arrives. Skip any of the three and users will see broken, confusing interfaces.

storyBeats.speaker: The three-state fetch pattern

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a <PostViewer postId /> component that fetches a post from https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/{postId}.

  • While loading: render <p data-testid="loading">Loading...</p>
  • On error: render <p data-testid="error">Failed to load post.</p>
  • On success: render a <div data-testid="post"> containing an <h2> with the post's title and a <p> with the post's body
  • Re-fetch whenever postId changes
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a <UserList> component from scratch. Fetch all users from https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users once on mount. Show a loading state, error state, and on success render each user's name and email in a list. Include a Retry button in the error state that re-triggers the fetch.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the three-state data-fetching pattern. What state variables do you need, what are their initial values, and why? What breaks if you forget to reset the error state before re-fetching? What is a race condition in this context, and how does a cleanup flag prevent it?

questions.prompt: Why can't you make the useEffect callback itself an async function?
options: An async function returns a Promise, but useEffect expects either nothing or a cleanup function
async/await is not supported inside React hooks
It would cause the component to suspend rendering
Async callbacks are not supported in JavaScript functions
questions.answer: An async function returns a Promise, but useEffect expects either nothing or a cleanup function
questions.explanation: useEffect's return value is treated as a cleanup function. If you return a Promise (by making the effect async), React doesn't know how to call it as a cleanup. The fix: define an async function inside the effect and call it immediately — the effect itself remains synchronous.

questions.prompt: The Fetch API does not throw an error for 4xx or 5xx HTTP responses. How do you handle this?
options: Check `res.ok` and throw manually: `if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status)`
The fetch Promise rejects automatically for any non-2xx response
Use res.status === 200 to check before calling res.json()
Wrap the entire fetch in a try/catch — it will catch HTTP errors automatically
questions.answer: Check `res.ok` and throw manually: `if (!res.ok) throw new Error('HTTP ' + res.status)`
questions.explanation: fetch() only rejects its Promise for network failures. A 404 or 500 response resolves successfully with res.ok === false. You must check res.ok and throw to route those cases into your catch block.

questions.prompt: After a failed fetch, the user retries. They see the old error flash before the new loading state appears. What is the cause?
options: The error state is not reset at the start of the new fetch
The retry button is rendering a new component instance
React batches the state updates and applies loading last
questions.answer: The error state is not reset at the start of the new fetch
questions.explanation: Always reset both at the start of every fetch: setLoading(true); setError(null). If error is not cleared, the component may briefly show both loading and error states.

questions.prompt: A user quickly switches between two userId values. Without a cleanup flag, what can go wrong?
options: Both requests complete, but the slower one may resolve last and overwrite the result for userId=2 with data for userId=1
React cancels the first fetch automatically when userId changes
The component will throw a runtime error due to two concurrent state updates
Both results are displayed simultaneously, causing a duplicate render
questions.answer: Both requests complete, but the slower one may resolve last and overwrite the result for userId=2 with data for userId=1
questions.explanation: This is a race condition. The cleanup flag (let cancelled = true in cleanup) prevents the stale response from calling setState after the component has moved on to a new userId.
